summary.text: Writing the factors in terms of \(A=1+x\), \(B=y+z\), and \(C=y-z\), the proof expands \((A+B)^{2n}(A^2-C^2)^n\); the three exponent constraints collapse the resulting fivefold coefficient sum to a double binomial sum. A trinomial-coefficient rearrangement reduces its inner sum to the alternating convolution read from \((1-t)^n(1+t)^n=(1-t^2)^n\), and Vandermonde’s identity \(\sum_j\binom nj^2=\binom{2n}n\) evaluates the remaining outer sum.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P_n(x,y,z)=(1+x+y+z)^{2n}(1+x+y-z)^n(1+x-y+z)^n.
\]
We prove, for every integer \(n\ge 0\), that
\[
[x^ny^nz^n]P_n(x,y,z)=\binom{2n}{n}^3.
\]
All polynomial coefficients are taken over \(\mathbb Z\). We use the usual convention that \(\binom ab=0\) if \(b>a\).

Put
\[
A=1+x,\qquad B=y+z,\qquad C=y-z.
\]
Then the three factors in \(P_n\) are respectively \(A+B\), \(A+C\), and \(A-C\). First combine the latter two factors:
\[
(A+C)^n(A-C)^n=(A^2-C^2)^n.
\]
Expanding this and also expanding \((A+B)^{2n}\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_n
&=(A+B)^{2n}(A^2-C^2)^n\\
&=\sum_{i=0}^{2n}\sum_{j=0}^n
 \binom{2n}{i}\binom nj(-1)^j
 A^{(2n-i)+2(n-j)}B^iC^{2j}\\
&=\sum_{i=0}^{2n}\sum_{j=0}^n
 \binom{2n}{i}\binom nj(-1)^j
 A^{4n-i-2j}B^iC^{2j}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This identity follows directly from the binomial theorem; the exponent \(4n-i-2j\) is nonnegative because \(i\le 2n\) and \(j\le n\).

We now extract the desired coefficient from a typical summand. For fixed \(i,j\), expand its three polynomial powers as
\[
(1+x)^{4n-i-2j}
 =\sum_{k=0}^{4n-i-2j}\binom{4n-i-2j}{k}x^k,
\]
\[
(y+z)^i=\sum_{u=0}^i\binom iu y^u z^{i-u},
\]
and
\[
(y-z)^{2j}=\sum_{v=0}^{2j}\binom{2j}{v}(-1)^{2j-v}y^v z^{2j-v}.
\]
Thus the monomial indexed by \((i,j,k,u,v)\) has exponents
\[
x^k y^{u+v}z^{i-u+2j-v}.
\]
It contributes to \(x^ny^nz^n\) precisely when
\[
k=n,\qquad u+v=n,\qquad i-u+2j-v=n. \tag{1}
\]
The second equation gives \(u=n-v\), and in particular requires \(v\le n\). Substituting \(u+v=n\) into the third equation gives
\[
i+2j-(u+v)=n,
\]
so
\[
i=2n-2j.
\]
Conversely, if \(0\le j\le n\), \(0\le v\le 2j\), \(v\le n\), and we set
\[
k=n,\qquad u=n-v,
\qquad i=2n-2j,
\]
then equations (1) hold whenever the indicated binomial terms are nonzero. If, for example, \(u>i\), then \(\binom{i}{u}=0\), so retaining such an index causes no difficulty. This is the standard zero-extension convention for binomial sums.

For the forced value \(i=2n-2j\), we have
\[
4n-i-2j=2n,
\]
and by symmetry
\[
\binom{2n}{i}=\binom{2n}{2n-2j}=\binom{2n}{2j}.
\]
Also, since \(0\le v\le 2j\), the integers \(2j-v\) and \(v\) have the same parity, and hence
\[
(-1)^{2j-v}=(-1)^v.
\]
It follows that the desired coefficient is the finite double sum
\[
\begin{aligned}
[x^ny^nz^n]P_n
={}&\sum_{j=0}^n\ \sum_{\substack{0\le v\le 2j\\v\le n}}
 \binom{2n}{2j}\binom nj(-1)^j
 \binom{2n}{n}\\
&\hspace{35mm}\cdot
 \binom{2n-2j}{n-v}\binom{2j}{v}(-1)^v. \tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]
We next evaluate this sum.

We need the binomial identity
\[
\binom{2n}{2j}\binom{2n-2j}{n-v}\binom{2j}{v}
=
\binom{2n}{n}\binom nv\binom n{2j-v}, \tag{3}
\]
valid for \(0\le j\le n\), \(0\le v\le 2j\), and \(v\le n\).

Here is a direct explanation of (3). Both sides count decompositions of a fixed \(2n\)-element set into four labeled blocks of respective sizes
\[
v,\qquad 2j-v,\qquad n-v,\qquad n-2j+v.
\]
For the left side, first choose the union of the first two blocks, of size \(2j\); choose the first block, of size \(v\), inside it; and choose the third block, of size \(n-v\), from the remaining \(2n-2j\) elements. For the right side, first choose the union of the first and third blocks, of size \(n\); choose the first block, of size \(v\), inside that chosen \(n\)-set; and choose the second block, of size \(2j-v\), from its \(n\)-element complement. If the last displayed block size \(n-2j+v\) is negative, then on the left \(n-v>2n-2j\), while on the right \(2j-v>n\); consequently both sides are zero. Thus (3) also covers that boundary case.

Substituting (3) into (2) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
[x^ny^nz^n]P_n
&=\binom{2n}{n}^2
 \sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj(-1)^j
 \sum_{\substack{0\le v\le 2j\\v\le n}}
 \binom nv\binom n{2j-v}(-1)^v. \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
The restriction \(v\le n\) in the inner sum may now be removed: whenever \(v>n\), the factor \(\binom nv\) is zero. Hence the inner sum in (4) is
\[
S_j:=\sum_{v=0}^{2j}(-1)^v\binom nv\binom n{2j-v}. \tag{5}
\]

We evaluate this alternating convolution by the binomial theorem. The coefficient of \(t^v\) in \((1-t)^n\) is \((-1)^v\binom nv\), and the coefficient of \(t^{2j-v}\) in \((1+t)^n\) is \(\binom n{2j-v}\). Therefore the product rule for coefficients shows that (5) is the coefficient of \(t^{2j}\) in
\[
(1-t)^n(1+t)^n=(1-t^2)^n.
\]
But
\[
(1-t^2)^n=\sum_{r=0}^n(-1)^r\binom nr t^{2r},
\]
so
\[
S_j=(-1)^j\binom nj. \tag{6}
\]
This remains valid at every endpoint, including \(j=0\) and \(j=n\).

Using (6) in (4), the two signs cancel:
\[
\begin{aligned}
[x^ny^nz^n]P_n
&=\binom{2n}{n}^2
 \sum_{j=0}^n \binom nj(-1)^j
 \left((-1)^j\binom nj\right)\\
&=\binom{2n}{n}^2
 \sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj^2. \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally, Vandermonde's identity in the central case gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj^2=\binom{2n}{n}. \tag{8}
\]
For completeness, (8) follows by taking the coefficient of \(t^n\) in
\[
(1+t)^n(1+t)^n=(1+t)^{2n}.
\]
The left side gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj\binom n{n-j}
=\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj^2,
\]
using \(\binom n{n-j}=\binom nj\), while the right side gives \(\binom{2n}{n}\).

Combining (7) and (8), we obtain
\[
[x^ny^nz^n]P_n
=\binom{2n}{n}^2\binom{2n}{n}
=\binom{2n}{n}^3.
\]
The argument also includes \(n=0\): then every sum has its sole index equal to zero, and both sides are \(1\). Therefore, for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
\boxed{\binom{2n}{n}^3=[x^ny^nz^n](1+x+y+z)^{2n}(1+x+y-z)^n(1+x-y+z)^n.}
\]
